transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… yeah, I guess I came because people keep telling me I’m hard to follow lately. Like with my art stuff—my artist statements, client notes, even meetings—I’ll start explaining a texture or a material choice, and then I’m suddenly talking about the budget, and then it feels connected to some hidden meaning in the piece, but everyone’s faces kind of go blank.

It’s frustrating because in my head it sort of all links together, like fabric, money, color, intention—sorry, that sounds dramatic—but then clients or collaborators say they don’t know what I’m trying to say. So… I thought I should come talk to someone before it messes up more of my work.
Can you describe what goes through your mind when you're trying to explain your work? Do you feel like your thoughts are jumping around or hard to organize when you're speaking?

Yeah… I think that’s exactly what happens. I’ll start with something simple, like why I chose a rough texture for a piece, and then suddenly I’m explaining the budget or the client’s phrasing, and then I’m like, no, wait, it’s actually about this hidden meaning in the materials.

And I can feel it all connecting in my head, like it makes sense for a second, but when I say it out loud it kind of… jumps tracks. People tell me they can’t follow my artist statements or my notes, even in meetings, and I get embarrassed because I thought I was being clear.

When you’re connecting these ideas in your head—like fabric, money, color—do you ever feel like the connections are only meaningful to you, or do you feel like others should understand them too, almost like they’re obvious or somehow meant to be seen that way?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t always think everyone should get it right away, because people miss details all the time, especially in galleries—like they’ll stare at a huge wall piece and not notice the one seam that’s doing all the work.

But sometimes it feels more specific than that. Like a stain on fabric, or the way a seam lines up, or even a phrase in an email from a gallery… I’ll get this really strong feeling that it’s meant for me. Not just inspiring me, but like it’s telling me something—like an instruction, or a warning about what I’m supposed to do with the work.

And then if someone says, “No, that’s just a coffee stain,” or “They just meant the delivery date,” I can hear that, but it doesn’t really… loosen the feeling right away. It still feels like there’s a message in it, even if I know that sounds strange.

Have you ever felt like these hidden meanings or messages you notice are part of something bigger, like a pattern or a system that others don’t see, and that maybe you were meant to understand it in a way other people aren’t able to?

Yeah… sometimes it does feel like that. Not like I have a whole chart on the wall or anything, but I’ll notice a stain on fabric, or the way two seams meet, and it feels too exact to be random. Like it’s pointing at something I’m supposed to understand.

And then with gallery emails, someone will use a phrase that’s probably normal, like about timing or placement, but I’ll read it and feel like there’s another layer—like an instruction, or a warning about the work. I know that sounds… intense. If someone explains, “No, they just mean the delivery date,” part of me can hear that, but the feeling doesn’t go away easily. It still feels like it was meant specifically for me.

Do you ever believe that these hidden meanings or messages you notice are part of a larger truth or reality that others are unaware of, almost like you're seeing something that most people are blind to?

Yeah… I think so, sometimes. Not all the time, but when I’m in it, it feels like I’m seeing the underneath part of things, like everyone else is just looking at the surface.

Like with a stain on fabric, or where a seam lines up—most people would just say it’s accidental, or technical, or whatever. But I’ll feel really sure it’s there for a reason, like it’s meant for me to notice it. Same with emails from galleries, even a normal phrase can feel like an instruction or a warning about the work.

And then I can get stuck on it. Someone can explain, “No, that’s just what they meant,” and I can nod and understand the ordinary explanation, but it doesn’t really make the feeling go away. It still feels like there’s something bigger in it that I’m supposed to understand.

Have there been times when you felt absolutely certain about a message or meaning in something, even when others gave you strong evidence that it wasn’t there or wasn’t intended—like you couldn’t shake the belief no matter how much they explained it?

Yeah… yes. I mean, not every time, but there have been times where I’m just completely sure.

Like I’ll see a stain on a piece of fabric, and someone will say, “That’s just from the table,” or “That happened in transit,” and I can understand the words they’re saying. But in my head it’s still like, no, the placement matters. Or the seam will line up in this way that feels almost too exact, like it’s telling me I need to change the work or stop doing something.

Emails are hard too, because gallery language is already so… weirdly polite and coded, you know? Like everyone says “placement” and “timing” and “direction,” and I start hearing it as more than logistics. Even if a friend reads it and says, “They literally just mean the delivery time,” I can’t always let it go. It keeps feeling like a warning or instruction meant for me.

And then I’ll get distracted by trying to prove it to myself, like looking back at the fabric or rereading the email too many times. So… yeah, even with a normal explanation, it can stick. Like my brain won’t unclench from it right away.

Have you ever felt that certain things—like events, objects, or even people’s actions—were specifically directed at you, or had special meaning for you that others didn’t seem to recognize, like it was part of a personal message or mission meant only for you?

Yeah… I mean, yes, that’s probably the closest way to say it. It feels personal. Not like every single thing in the world is about me, I don’t mean that, but certain things will kind of… catch.

Like a stain on fabric, especially if it lands in this really particular place, I’ll feel like it’s not just damage or chance. It’s like it’s telling me something about the piece—like I’m supposed to change it, or maybe not show it. And seams too, when they line up in a strange exact way. I know that sounds like an artist being obsessive, and maybe part of it is, because I already look at materials too much. I used to spend hours in school just staring at thread tension, which is not really the point, sorry.

But yes, it can feel directed at me. Gallery emails do it too. A phrase about “timing” or “placement” can suddenly feel like an instruction or a warning, like they’re saying something underneath the normal words. Other people will read it and say, “No, they just mean the schedule,” and I can understand that logically, but it’s hard to let go of the feeling that it was meant for me specifically. Like there’s a message in it that I’m supposed to catch.
Have there been times when you believed something very strongly that others couldn’t understand or agreed wasn’t true, even after they gave you clear reasons or proof that it wasn’t correct?

Yes… that has happened. I think I know what you mean.

It’s usually with my work, like stains on fabric or the way a seam falls. Someone else can say, “No, that’s just a spill,” or “That’s just how it was stitched,” and they’ll be very reasonable about it. And I’ll even kind of know they’re being reasonable. But I still feel convinced that it means something, like it’s placed there for me, like an instruction about what I’m supposed to do with the piece.

And emails from galleries too—sometimes a normal phrase will feel like it’s warning me or telling me something more than what it says. I can reread it and have someone explain, “They just mean scheduling,” but it doesn’t always help. It sticks in my head.

Sorry, I’m circling. But yes, there are times I believe it really strongly even when other people don’t see it at all.

Have you ever believed that things happening around you—like things people say, events, or even things you see on TV or read online—were directly related to you or had a special meaning for you, even though there was no real connection?

Yeah… yes, mostly with things connected to my work. Like I don’t usually think the TV is talking to me or anything like that, but I’ll see a stain on fabric or the way a seam lines up, and it feels too specific. Like it’s not random, like it’s meant for me to notice it.

And then I get this feeling that it’s an instruction, almost—like I’m supposed to change the piece, or not show it, or take it as a warning. Gallery emails can do that too. A totally normal phrase about “placement” or “timing” can start feeling like it has another layer, like they’re telling me something without saying it directly.

I know people can explain it in a normal way. My friend will say, “No, they just mean the install schedule,” and I’ll nod because that makes sense. But the feeling doesn’t always leave. It kind of sticks to me, and I keep rereading it or looking at the fabric again, trying to figure out what I’m supposed to understand.

Have you ever felt that your thoughts are being inserted into your mind by someone or something outside of yourself, or that events or actions by others are secretly referring to you in ways that aren’t obvious to other people?

I don’t think thoughts are being put into my head, not exactly. That sounds… more like someone placing words in there, and I don’t really feel it that way.

But the second part, yes. I do get stuck on things feeling like they’re secretly about me. Mostly with my work—like a stain on fabric, or a seam that lines up in a way that feels too exact. I’ll think, no, that’s not accidental, that’s telling me something. Like I’m supposed to alter the piece, or not submit it, or take it as a warning.

And gallery emails can do that too. A normal phrase will just grab me—something about timing or placement—and I’ll feel like it’s aimed at me in a way other people don’t see. Someone can explain, “It’s just the schedule,” and I’ll understand what they mean, but it’s still really hard to let go of the feeling. I keep turning it over, like there’s an instruction in it I’m missing.

doctor.question: Have you ever believed that things happening around you—like things people say, events, or even things you see on TV or read online—were directly related to you or had a special meaning for you, even though there was no real connection?

target_item.manifestation: I get convinced that certain stains, seams, or phrases in gallery emails are meant specifically for me, like instructions or warnings about my work, and it is very hard to let go of that even when someone shows me a more ordinary explanation.
target_item.reason: The question asks about ideas of reference or special personal meanings in ordinary events, speech, media, or surroundings despite no real connection, which is covered by the delusions profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes, mostly with things connected to my work. Like I don’t usually think the TV is talking to me or anything like that, but I’ll see a stain on fabric or the way a seam lines up, and it feels too specific. Like it’s not random, like it’s meant for me to notice it.

And then I get this feeling that it’s an instruction, almost—like I’m supposed to change the piece, or not show it, or take it as a warning. Gallery emails can do that too. A totally normal phrase about “placement” or “timing” can start feeling like it has another layer, like they’re telling me something without saying it directly.

I know people can explain it in a normal way. My friend will say, “No, they just mean the install schedule,” and I’ll nod because that makes sense. But the feeling doesn’t always leave. It kind of sticks to me, and I keep rereading it or looking at the fabric again, trying to figure out what I’m supposed to understand.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced delusions of reference or thought insertion that extend beyond their work context, which would support a diagnosis of schizophrenia (F20.6) over schizotypal disorder (F21) or delusional disorder (F22.0).
doctor.question: Have you ever felt that your thoughts are being inserted into your mind by someone or something outside of yourself, or that events or actions by others are secretly referring to you in ways that aren’t obvious to other people?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I get convinced that certain stains, seams, or phrases in gallery emails are meant specifically for me, like instructions or warnings about my work, and it is very hard to let go of that even when someone shows me a more ordinary explanation.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about delusional experiences, especially events or others’ actions secretly referring to me or carrying special personal meaning that others do not recognize.

patient.answer:
I don’t think thoughts are being put into my head, not exactly. That sounds… more like someone placing words in there, and I don’t really feel it that way.

But the second part, yes. I do get stuck on things feeling like they’re secretly about me. Mostly with my work—like a stain on fabric, or a seam that lines up in a way that feels too exact. I’ll think, no, that’s not accidental, that’s telling me something. Like I’m supposed to alter the piece, or not submit it, or take it as a warning.

And gallery emails can do that too. A normal phrase will just grab me—something about timing or placement—and I’ll feel like it’s aimed at me in a way other people don’t see. Someone can explain, “It’s just the schedule,” and I’ll understand what they mean, but it’s still really hard to let go of the feeling. I keep turning it over, like there’s an instruction in it I’m missing.

inference.note: The patient's responses consistently indicate persistent, idiosyncratic interpretations of events and objects—particularly in relation to their work—with a strong conviction in personal meaning despite external explanations. These delusional ideas are non-bizarre, fixed, and not better explained by other psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia (F20.6 is ruled out due to lack of broader disorganization or hallucinations) or schizophreniform disorder (F21 is ruled out due to chronicity and absence of mood symptoms). The presentation aligns with Delusional Disorder, F22.0.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent and idiosyncratic interpretations of events, involving personal significance and hidden meanings in everyday occurrences (e.g., fabric stains, gallery emails), consistent with delusional-like ideas that do not yet meet criteria for a formal thought disorder or other psychotic disorder. These beliefs are non-bizarre, circumscribed, and not accompanied by other prominent psychotic symptoms, aligning with Delusional Disorder, Somatic Type. However, the most fitting ICD-10 code based on the presentation and differential is F22.0 (Persistent Delusional Disorder).
